cues.text: Brother of the Lord
James, described in Scripture as "the Lord's brother" and distinct in lists from James the son of Alphaeus, has long been identified by Church tradition with him mentioned by St.
Paul — though the precise relationships among the New Testament's several men named James remain historically debated, and this venerable identification is not free of scholarly question.
Tradition holds him a close kinsman of Jesus, whether cousin or another form of near relation, according to the wide flexibility of the term "brother" in the Semitic usage of the day.

Called to the Apostolate alongside his own brother Jude, James is named at the head of the third group in every listing of the Twelve, and though the Gospels tell us little of his individual words during Christ's public ministry, his later prominence in the Jerusalem Church shows a man whose formation at Jesus's side had prepared him for extraordinary responsibility.
Witness of the Risen Christ
St.

Paul records a detail found nowhere else in the New Testament: that the Risen Christ appeared personally to James, a private encounter significant enough that Paul lists it separately from the general appearances to the assembled Apostles.

Whatever passed between them in that meeting, its effect was unmistakable: James emerges immediately afterward as one of the recognized "pillars" of the early Jerusalem community, trusted enough by Paul himself, on his very first visit to Jerusalem after his conversion, to be sought out alongside Peter as one of the two authoritative voices Paul most needed to consult.
The First Bishop of Jerusalem

Ancient and consistent tradition, recorded by Eusebius drawing on even earlier sources, holds that James was appointed by the Apostles themselves as the first bishop of the mother Church of Jerusalem , governing that community — still composed almost entirely of converts from Judaism — through its earliest and most delicate years, when the relationship between the young Church and the wider Jewish community remained unresolved and often tense.

James's own manner of life, marked by intense asceticism and constant prayer in the Temple, earned him such a reputation for holiness that even Jews who had not embraced the Gospel are said to have called him James the Just , and to have shown him a respect that, later tradition holds, extended even to touching the hem of his garment in veneration.
Opening the Church to the Gentile World

James's most consequential act as bishop came at the Council of Jerusalem around the year 50, where the Apostles and elders gathered to resolve the urgent question of whether Gentile converts needed to be circumcised and bound to the full observance of Mosaic Law.

After Peter, and then Paul and Barnabas, testified to the Spirit's evident work among Gentile believers, it was James — as the leading figure of the Jerusalem church, and a man whose own personal fidelity to Jewish practice was well established — who proposed the final formulation, proposing the compromise that freed Gentile Christians from the full ceremonial Law while asking a few reasonable accommodations in return.

That single ruling, carried by James's own particular authority and credibility, opened the Christian faith definitively and permanently to the whole non-Jewish world, a decision without which the Church as we know it today could scarcely have come into being.
A Faith Proved by Works

James left the Church a short but forceful epistle, addressed to the whole scattered community of Jewish Christians, insisting with characteristic bluntness that genuine faith must show itself in concrete deeds of charity and integrity — faith without works is dead — a teaching that has echoed through every century since as an essential corrective against any Christianity content merely to profess belief while neglecting the poor, the vulnerable, and the plain demands of a converted life.
Legacy

James governed the Jerusalem Church for roughly three decades, through years of growing tension between Christians and the wider Jewish establishment, until, according to the Church's ancient tradition, he was seized around the year 62, thrown from the parapet of the Temple, and beaten to death when the fall failed to kill him outright; Josephus instead reports that he was condemned and stoned.

The first bishop of the Church's mother see, and author of one of the New Testament's most searching calls to a lived, active faith, James, often identified in tradition as James the Less, of the quiet, steady episcopal governance that held the earliest Church together through its most uncertain years — proof that holiness expressed in patient, faithful leadership can be every bit as consequential as the more dramatic missionary journeys of his fellow Apostles.
